item.content:encoded:
Red Label Day For D2C Brands 

India’s food industry is facing its biggest labelling overhaul in years. The SC has directed the FSSAI to ensure that packaged foods carry separate pictorial warnings for high fat, sugar and salt, along with red labels as caution for customers. So, what does the latest ruling mean for clean-label D2C food brands?

Tighter Labelling Norms: Rejecting FSSAI’s single-badge proposal, the SC has ruled that packaged foods, which exceed prescribed thresholds, must display separate hexagonal pictorial warnings for high fat, sugar or salt. The court also urged the Centre to embed nutritional literacy into school curricula through interactive workshops.

A Long-Drawn Battle: FSSAI initially had pitched a health-star rating plan (akin to Bureau of Energy Efficiency’s star label on appliances), but the plan did not translate into a mandatory regime. It then pivoted towards red hexagonal labels, but faced swift pushback from industry players. With SC now offering clarity, D2C brands have no recourse but to comply. 

Implications For Brands: For new-age D2C food brands built on “healthy” and “clean-label” positioning, front-of-pack warnings could threaten core brand equity. Meeting stricter norms could lead to costly recipe re-formulations, packaging redesigns and tweaked marketing. The challenge will also be balancing health claims with regulatory compliance, while keeping costs and margins in check.

Trust Needs Proof: Experts had previously told Inc42 that the crackdown could potentially create a better opportunity for brands to demonstrate better ingredients, transparent formulations and verifiable nutritional claims. However, it will raise the cost of entering the category and threaten the marketing language that helped many D2C brands grow

As India moves towards stricter front-of-pack labelling, will D2C brands adapt their products and messaging fast enough to stay ahead of the curve? While that is a question for another day, here is all about SC’s observation on what a product label should look like…

From The Editor’s Desk

Startups Rethink Compute Cost

  • Rising memory chip prices and tightening GPU availability are driving up infrastructure costs for Indian AI and SaaS companies, forcing businesses to rethink their computing requirements
  • Higher compute costs, longer GPU rental commitments and rising cloud bills threaten startup profitability, capital efficiency and the commercial viability of AI products
  • As many vendors push Indian startups towards six-month rental commitments, platforms are exploring domain-specific AI models, quantisation and efficient infrastructure deployment to contain costs.

Finnable Nets ₹405 Cr

  • The digital lending startup has raised around $44 Mn in its Series C round led by Bharat Value Fund to expand its lending portfolio, strengthen its tech stack and forge new partnerships across the lending ecosystem.
  • Founded in 2015, Finnable offers personal loans to mid-income salaried professionals. Its consolidated AUM stood at over ₹4,600 Cr at the end of October. The startup also reported a profit of ₹51 Cr in H1 FY27. 
  • Finnable’s latest fundraise comes amid continued investor interest in the Indian lending tech market, which is seeing lenders use technology to facilitate credit for borrowers that remain underserved by traditional banking channels

UC’s Latest Experiment

  • Urban Company has now forayed into the residential AC market. The startup has opened pre-bookings for its new product lines, Native AC Ultra and Ultra Air, exclusively on its app. The price of the ACs will start from ₹55,499.
  • This comes nearly a year after Inc42 first reported on the company’s plans to enter the residential AC market. With this, the listed company will look to expand its Native brand beyond water purifiers and smart locks. 
  • The latest product launch comes even as Urban Company continues to bleed amid rising investments in its quick service vertical. UC’s net loss more than tripled YoY to ₹182.5 Cr in Q2 FY27, while operating revenue rose 41.4% YoY to ₹537.3 Cr. 

IndiaMART-OpenAI Settle Dispute

  • The B2B ecommerce company has settled its legal dispute with the AI giant. The out-of-court settlement of the case, which was listed in front of the Calcutta High Court, brings the matter to a close after about two years of proceedings.
  • The case pertained to alleged exclusion of IndiaMART’s website and seller listings from ChatGPT-generated responses. The listed company had also alleged that the selective exclusion had caused it reputational damage, loss of goodwill and commercial injury. 
  • The relief comes as OpenAI continues to juggle multiple legal cases in India. Previously, news agency ANI and multiple book publishers had dragged the AI giant to court over alleged unauthorised use of their copyrighted material for training ChatGPT.

ElecBits Eyes $15 Mn 

  • The electronics design and manufacturing startup is in talks to raise $12 Mn to $15 Mn in a fresh funding round led by PE firm Xponentia Capital. Existing backer Nexus Venture Partners is also expected to participate in the fundraise.
  • Founded in 2019, Elecbits designs, manufactures and delivers hardware products for businesses. It also operates an AI-powered platform that offers instant quotations, supply chain visibility and risk management tools. It last raised $5.5 Mn in 2025.
  • The fundraise comes amid growing investments in the local electronics manufacturing ecosystem, which is being driven by government subsidies, rising demand and the need to secure electronics supply chain amid rising geopolitical tensions. 

India’s AI Push Gathers Steam

  • Chariot AI has unveiled its first indigenous AI model suite under the IndiaAI Mission. The suite comprises a mixture-of-experts AI model, which comes in four variants – 10.7 Bn, 1.7 Bn and 745 Mn parameters. It also debuted a text-to-speech model.
  • Separately, BharatGen also rolled out Patram 1.5, a vision-language model aimed at automating document processing for BFSI, government and other enterprise workflows. This expands the startup’s AI model portfolio beyond text and speech. 
  • The launches come as investors continue to make a beeline for the Indian enterprise AI sector as a new crop of startups look to automate workflows across varied enterprise use cases. The space is projected to become a $71 Bn opportunity by 2030.

Inc42 Markets

Inc42 Startup Spotlight

How Karta AI Is Automating The BFSI Customer Service

When a user calls about a failed payment or a delayed loan, an agent often has to verify identity, retrieve data from multiple systems and complete several steps. This slows down resolution and increases costs. Karta AI is building voice AI agents that can automate these complex calls end to end.

Built For Complexity: Founded in 2024, Karta AI offers a customer communication platform across voice, chat, email and WhatsApp. Its AI agents use a predictive context engine that draws on a business’ knowledge bases, past interactions and live enterprise data to handle multiple customer intents rather than routing callers to other agents. It escalates the call to a human only when necessary. 

Growing Market Traction: The startup claims that it handles around 20 Lakh customer conversations every month across 25+ languages. It also claims to have 10–12 paying customers, including PhonePe, Pine Labs, Bajaj and Aavas. Karta also claims that its inbound servicing agent resolves about 70% of borrower queries end-to-end cuts cost per query by nearly 50%. 

What’s On The Horizon? Backed by PeerCapital, the startup now plans to further strengthen its end-to-end automation and multilingual capabilities, expand BFSI deployments, and grow its engineering and GTM teams. Its next challenge will be maintaining accuracy, security and compliance while handling increasingly sensitive financial workflows. 

With India’s conversational AI market projected to become a $3.7 Bn opportunity by 2033, can Karta AI make voice agents the default layer for BFSI customer service?

item.title: Apple To Open Seventh India Store In Hyderabad’s Kukatpally
item.dc:creator: Team Inc42
item.description: Apple continues to expand its retail footprint in India. The iPhone maker is all set to launch its seventh official…
item.content:encoded:
Apple continues to expand its retail footprint in India. The iPhone maker is all set to launch its seventh official store in the country in Hyderabad on December 10.

As per its website, the new store will open at Lake Shore Mall in Hyderabad’s Kukatpally. The new outlet will offer the complete lineup of Apple products and services, including the latest iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone Duo, MacBook Pro, Apple Watches, AirPods and HomePods.

According to Deccan Herald, the company has also revealed the barricade for the Kukatpally store, which features a pearl-inspired Apple logo set against iridescent tones. It takes inspiration from the city’s historical title as the City of Pearls. 

The new outlet will join the company’s six other flagship stores in the country. The Cupertino-based big tech giant already operates retail outlets in Mumbai’s BKC and Borivali, Saket and Noida in Delhi NCR, Hebbal in Bengaluru and Koregaon Park in Pune. 

Notably, Apple already has a healthy presence in the city. Hyderabad is home to the company’s retail customer team and the R&D division for maps. 

The move comes as Apple continues to deepen its presence in India by launching retail outlets, leasing spaces for corporate offices and scaling local manufacturing.

In January this year, the iPhone maker leased an additional 57,000 sq ft of office space at WaveRock IT Park in Hyderabad for five years at a monthly rent of ₹71.6 Lakh. With this, the total footprint of its campus in the city now stands at nearly 6.34 Lakh sq ft.

A week ago, Apple also reportedly opened its second office in Bengaluru. Located at Embassy Zenith in the startup hub’s Vasanth Nagar, the 14-story building stands directly opposite the 150-year-old Bangalore Golf Club.

Not just this, the company is also aggressively doubling down on manufacturing in India. The country has become one of its largest production bases outside China, with iPhone exports crossing ₹2 Lakh Cr in FY26. 

At the same time, it is also expanding its services ecosystem in India. The OEM has launched new offerings such as Apple Pay and Fitness+ in the past few months, which are expected to create new revenue streams for the iPhone maker going forward.

All these bets appear to be paying off. Buoyed by strong demand across iPhones, Macs, iPads and other products, Apple India’s net profit zoomed 66% YoY to ₹5,311 Cr in FY26 as operating revenue grew 31.4% YoY to ₹1.04 Lakh Cr.

The original equipment manufacturer (OEM) also reported record India revenues in Q4 FY26, with its iPhone vertical setting a revenue record and Mac and services revenue reaching new highs.

However, near-term momentum faces pressure due to chip and memory shortages. The company recently said that it expects supply chain constraints to impact iPhones, Macs and iPads globally, potentially influencing product availability in India.

In another headwind, the iPhone maker Apple also suffered a major outage earlier this month, which brought many of its services to a standstill for thousands of users globally.

item.title: WhatsApp To Partner Jio To Launch Int’l Data eSIM Feature In India
item.dc:creator: Team Inc42
item.description: Messaging platform WhatsApp plans to roll out a new feature that lets users buy and install international data eSIMs directly…
item.content:encoded:
Messaging platform WhatsApp plans to roll out a new feature that lets users buy and install international data eSIMs directly within the app.

In a blog post, WhatsApp said that the offering will initially be available in select countries. The messaging giant said that it is also “working” with Indian telecom giant Reliance Jio for the launch. 

“To make it even easier to connect when traveling, today we’re announcing a new way to buy and install a data eSIM when traveling internationally in just a few taps without leaving the app. It’ll be as effortless as sending a message,” read the blog post.

According to news portal Android Authority, the code of WhatsApp’s app version 2.26.47.10 also contains references to a new feature that could help users buy eSIMs. As per the report, the messaging platform will search for compatible eSIM options once users enter their destination.

The tool will reportedly also allow users to view their purchased and expired eSIMs and check their remaining data balance. The aforementioned version of WhatsApp also reportedly appears capable of warning users when they are running low on data and when their plan is about to expire.

Besides Jio, WhatsApp also said that it is also working with multiple eSIM providers and telecom operators, including Smart Axiata, Smart Communications and Verizon for the new offering. “You’ll see it right in the app when it’s available for you,” added WhatsApp.

“What if WhatsApp could work anywhere you go in the world without any struggle. Starting our early explorations around eSIMs so that you can continue sending those stickers without any interruptions… Inviting partners everywhere to join us in this important mission,” said WhatsApp CEO Kunal Shah in a post on X.

The latest launch comes as WhatsApp looks to expand beyond messaging under newly-appointed CEO Kunal Shah, who took over as the platform’s global head earlier this year after stepping away from day-to-day operations at CRED.

Just a day ago, the Meta-owned platform also introduced scheduled messages feature, which allows users to schedule texts, photos and videos in advance (between 10 minutes and 14 days) across individual and group chats. 

Earlier this month, Shah outlined three broad priorities for WhatsApp — making communication more expressive, simplifying everyday services and integrating AI into the platform. 

As part of this, the messaging giant is also streamlining offerings such as bill payments and financial transactions within WhatsApp. It is also said to be piloting new features such as view-once text messages in the app on select Android devices. 

Overall, India is the biggest market for WhatsApp in terms of customers, with the country accounting for more than 500 Mn of its global user base.

item.title: CERT-In Flags High-Severity Vulnerability In e-Governance Platform DIGIT
item.dc:creator: Gaurav Bagur
item.description: The Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) has issued a high-severity vulnerability note, warning about a SQL injection flaw in…
item.content:encoded:
The Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) has issued a high-severity vulnerability note, warning about a SQL injection flaw in open-source governance platform DIGIT. 

“This vulnerability exists in the DIGIT Platform due to improper neutralisation of user supplied input while constructing SQL queries and execution in the affected user and access control service components. An unauthenticated remote attacker could exploit this vulnerability by sending specially crafted input through the affected API endpoint to the targeted system,” noted the agency. 

The flaw could potentially allow remote cyberattackers to execute unauthorised SQL commands without prior access. Successful exploitation could allow them to manipulate application logic and modify, or delete, sensitive database information. 

However, the note does not indicate whether any attackers have exploited the vulnerability. 

The eGov Foundation, which operates the platform, has addressed the issue in DIGIT Core v2.9.3. The foundation has directed the platforms, running the affected deployments, to update immediately to the latest version to resolve the vulnerability, CERT-In added. 

DIGIT (Digital Infrastructure for Governance, Inclusion & Transformation) is an open-source platform created by eGov Foundation. Currently led by CEO Viraj Tyagi, a cofounder of fintech startup Finnable, the foundation was established in 2003 by Nandan Nilekani and Srikanth Nadhamuni to leverage technology for powering digital public and municipal services

The platform provides building blocks and shared data registries for building sector-specific digital public infrastructure (DPI). It enables local governments, civic bodies, ecosystem partners, and NGOs to rapidly deploy large-scale public service applications for use cases like water billing, digital health registries, business licensing systems, vaccination portals, and others.

Hence, in case the vulnerability was used to breach applications built on DIGIT’s platform, it could result in leaks of sensitive data and disruption of civic services. 

Rapid advances in frontier AI models have made it significantly easier for hackers and cyberattackers to exploit weaknesses in software. 

Recent disruptions involving the likes of Microsoft, Apple, JPMorgan Chase and the US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) have only shone a further spotlight on the risks posed by vulnerabilities in interconnected tech systems.

item.title: GEF Capital Partners Announces First Close Of India Climate Fund IV At $615 Mn
item.dc:creator: Anjali Jain
item.description: Climate focused PE firm GEF Capital Partners announced the first close of its fourth India-focused climate fund at $615 Mn,…
item.content:encoded:
Climate focused PE firm GEF Capital Partners announced the first close of its fourth India-focused climate fund at $615 Mn, exceeding its initial target.

The fundraise is approximately 40% larger than the firm’s previous $440 Mn fund, making it GEF Capital Partners’ largest fundraise to date. 

Fund IV will primarily target mid-market, growth-stage cleantech businesses operating India and South Asia.

The first close attracted a diverse pool of global institutional investors, including pension funds, sovereign investors, foundations and family offices. The fund’s limited partners are primarily based across Europe, Japan, the UK, Singapore and the US.

“India’s energy transition is increasingly becoming a driver of industrial growth and global competitiveness. We see significant opportunities in businesses that improve resource efficiency, accelerate electrification and strengthen sustainable supply chains,” said Raj Pai, cofounder and managing partner, GEF Capital Partners.

GEF Capital Partners’ existing India portfolio includes companies such as ReNew Power, Indian Energy Exchange, Premier Energies, Sterlite Electric, Sahyadri Farms, Arya.ag, TI Clean, Yulu Bikes and Hero Motors.

In August, the PE firm led Yulu’s $93 Mn Series C funding round, which followed its leading participation in agritech startup Arya.ag’s $80.58 Mn Series D round in April.  

India’s energy transition and sustainable industrial growth’s funding landscape has witnessed a sharp uptick in recent months, with cleantech startups raising $433 Mn across 23 deals in the third quarter of 2026, up 267% YoY compared to $118 Mn across 16 deals in the year-ago quarter.

A bulk of this growth has been driven by electric mobility investments, which accounted for over 70% of the total inflow during the quarter. The concentration in a handful of large electric mobility rounds, with investors increasingly emphasising unit economics, capital efficiency and the ability to scale.

item.title: [Update] Jio Takes JioAstro Offline, Says It Was A ‘Demo Survey’
item.dc:creator: Shrishti Bisht
item.description: Update | November 26, 19:47 IST Hours after Jio Platforms’ astrology platform JioAstro became publicly accessible, the company appears to…
item.content:encoded:
Update | November 26, 19:47 IST

Hours after Jio Platforms’ astrology platform JioAstro became publicly accessible, the company appears to have taken it offline. “Thank you for participating in the demo survey! It has now closed and is no longer available,” the website reads.

Sources told Inc42 that the platform was being tested privately and wasn’t supposed to be realised publicly. It remains unclear if Jio will make the offering publicly available at a later date.

Original | November 25, 18:19 IST

Telecom major Jio Platforms has forayed into online astrology market with the launch of a dedicated offering, JioAstro. 

JioAstro generates birth charts using “Swiss Ephemeris calculations” and further gives personalised insights by advanced AI trained in Vedic astrology. JioAstro is available in English, Hindi, Marathi and Gujarati. 

The company hasn’t disclosed which large language models (LLMs) power the platform, whether it relies on proprietary models or third-party AI infrastructure.

While JioAstro is accessible through its website and has a listing on Google Play, its terms describe the mobile app as an invite-only prototype available through the internal testing track.

With the AI-powered vedic astrology platform, Jio takes on the likes of consumer startups Astrotalk, AstroSage, among others, who have already been in this space for some years. 

One of the most renowned astrology platforms and India’s 133rd unicorn, Astrotalk, was delisted from Apple’s App Store on November 4. Sources told Inc42 that the spiritual tech startup is in discussions with Apple over the delisting. The app, however, remains unavailable on the platform.

The broader spiritual tech ecosystem has seen growing investor interest, with startups raising capital to expand their offerings.

Earlier this year, Astrotalk joined India’s unicorn club following an employee stock ownership plan (ESOP) buyback at a $1 Bn valuation. Back then, the startup also said its annual revenue run rate (ARR) had crossed ₹2,500 Cr.

Other startups like AppsForBharat, VAMA, MyNaksh, Sanctuary, AstroSure, among others, have also raised investor support in recent times. 

More recently, Kolkata-based Utsav raised ₹36 Cr ($3.8 Mn) in a Series A round led by Atomic Capital, with existing investors India Quotient and Equanimity Investments also participating.

The stars of the Indian digital astrology market are on the rise. The segment is estimated to be worth $390 Mn in 2026 and is projected to reach $2.32 Bn by 2032, registering a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 34.61%, as per MarkNtel Advisors.

item.title: Memory Costs Become A Headache. How Are Indian Startups Coping?
item.dc:creator: Shraddha Goled
item.description: Samsung’s entry-level Galaxy A07 5G now costs ₹22,999, up ₹2,000 from ₹20,999, under revised prices that took effect on November…
item.content:encoded:
Samsung’s entry-level Galaxy A07 5G now costs ₹22,999, up ₹2,000 from ₹20,999, under revised prices that took effect on November 16. And that’s not it. Eight days after Diwali, on November 15-16, the prices of around 48 Samsung and Xiaomi smartphone variants rose by ₹1,000-₹4,000. These price hikes are the result of the rising cost of memory chips and other components. 

But rising memory chip costs are now hurting more than just the consumer electronics industry. The ripple effects have extended well beyond chip giants like NVIDIA, AMD and Qualcomm, and cloud behemoths such as AWS, Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud. Consequently, cloud hosting, storage and hardware procurement costs have started to burn holes in the pockets of SaaS companies.

For Indian AI startups, too, rising memory costs means that building and running compute infrastructure is getting more expensive, even as limited GPU availability continues to delay deployments. 

For startups already investing heavily in AI capabilities, the memory crunch raises a pressing question. How are businesses factoring in the changing economics of computing? Let’s dive in…

When Compute Becomes A Bottleneck

For AI companies, memory is becoming a cost across the entire model lifecycle, from training and data storage to deployment and inference.

Training datasets need to be stored, versioned and kept close to computing infrastructure. As companies work with increasingly large volumes of text, images, audio and video, storage requirements grow. Once a model is deployed, platforms also accumulate user-generated data, including prompts, conversation histories, documents, embeddings and audit logs.

Inference, or the process of running a trained model to generate responses, adds another layer of memory requirements. Longer conversations and more users accessing a model simultaneously increase the memory needed to maintain the model’s key-value (KV) cache that stores information from earlier parts of a conversation so that the model can use it while generating subsequent responses.

But the pressure is not limited to memory prices alone. 

AI companies are also combating the rising cost and limited availability of GPUs, which are needed to run AI workloads (training and running the model).

Subhashish Banerjee, cofounder of Bharat1 AI, which works with startups and infrastructure providers, said the economics of accessing GPUs have changed sharply over the past few months. Earlier, some AI startups could book GPUs for a few hours each day, depending on availability and price, and run customer workloads during that window. That flexibility has reduced. 

According to him, GPU prices have risen 30-35% since February 2026, while availability has tightened. Startups that previously booked capacity for 10-11 hours at a time are being asked to commit for three or six months.

This has raised a new problem: companies are being asked to pay for capacity before they are sure customer demand will materialise. Simply put: A startup expecting to onboard a customer in June may have to reserve computing resources in March or January. 

Subhashish said the problem is particularly staring at smaller startups that lack the capital to make long-term commitments. However, this does not mean enterprises with deep pockets can avoid the shocks. 

A case in point is Bengaluru-based payments technology company Juspay, which reported a net loss of ₹90 Cr in FY26, compared with a net profit of ₹62 Cr in the previous year, as it stepped up investments in AI capabilities and international expansion. Its revenue, however, grew 30% to ₹664 Cr.

The company is also waiting for GPU capacity. Cofounder and COO Sheetal Lalwani said Juspay wants to increase its GPU investments but is constrained by allocation, with delivery commitments stretching three to six months. The company is awaiting a larger 72-GPU rack.

Then, Indian companies are vulnerable to currency fluctuations. “Almost all of our compute is bought in dollars, which compounds the problem. A price rise that hurts a US company hurts an Indian company more,” said Abhijeet Zilpelwar, the cofounder and CTO of pi-labs, an AI native cybersecurity company.

Cloud Over SaaS Profitability

Traditional SaaS companies are facing a different set of challenges. The pressure is growing as these businesses continue to add AI features to their products. While they are less exposed to rising memory costs than AI model developers, given their limited reliance on high-end GPUs and specialised memory chips, they are not immune to the broader cost pressures. 

Their dependence on cloud infrastructure, which runs on servers equipped with DRAM and storage systems using NAND flash, makes them vulnerable to rising memory costs. As cloud providers face higher infrastructure expenses, some of these costs get passed on to SaaS companies.

Applications that once relied largely on conventional computing now need additional capacity to process AI workloads, store larger volumes of data, and support inference. This can increase infrastructure spending even as companies try to keep subscription prices competitive.

The challenge is particularly acute for companies with fixed or per-seat subscription models. Their infrastructure costs can increase with usage, while revenue may not rise at the same pace. For smaller SaaS businesses already operating on thin margins, even a modest increase in hosting and storage expenses can make a difference.

The scale of the increase is visible in cloud spending. 

According to industry estimates cited by Financial Express, a growth stage Indian startup that spent ₹8-20 Lakh a month on cloud infrastructure two years ago now typically spends ₹18-45 Lakh. For late stage and enterprise-scale companies, monthly spending has risen from ₹50-80 Lakh to ₹1.5 Cr. These increases reflect the growing complexity of workloads, AI experimentation and GPU computing. 

But cloud providers are not necessarily passing every increase on to customers. CloudPe cofounder Karan Jaju said the company has kept prices for older-generation cloud instances unchanged, while newer configurations with updated CPUs and RAM have become more expensive. The pressure comes amid rising memory costs, with TrendForce forecasting computer memory, also called DRAM, contract prices to increase 10-15% quarter-on-quarter in Q4 2026. 

He added, new hardware (memory chips, CPUs, GPUs, etc.) purchases among some customers have fallen 5-10%. Some are instead exploring virtual desktop infrastructure (VDI), which lets employees access cloud-hosted desktops without companies having to buy and maintain physical machines.

Subhashish said Series B and Series C companies with substantial computing needs may consider buying hardware through infrastructure providers or loans, while earlier stage startups are likely to continue relying on cloud services and shorter-term rentals.

Smaller Models, Lighter Hardware

Another response to rising computing and memory requirements is to make AI models smaller and more efficient. This is happening not just among startups trying to reduce inference costs, but also among companies building AI features for consumer devices.

The shift towards smaller language models (SLMs) is helping companies run selected AI workloads on smartphones and laptops, instead of sending every request to large models hosted in data centres.

Google’s Gemini Nano, for instance, is designed to run directly on Android devices through its AICore system. It can support tasks such as summarisation and smart replies without sending every prompt to the cloud. Apple has made its on-device foundation model available to developers through its Foundation Models framework, while Microsoft’s Phi Silica is designed to run locally on Copilot+ PCs.

For AI application companies, another approach is to reduce the amount of computing required for every interaction.

Apurv Agrawal, the cofounder and CEO of SquadStack, a voice AI agent maker, said the company has managed to reduce its costs by moving away from general-purpose models for its core voice AI workloads.

SquadStack’s AI agents make more than 50 Lakh calls a day, often switching between Hindi, English and regional languages during conversations. The company built its own speech recognition model, Arth, trained on Indian phone audio, and its Sales LLM, Maya, which is post-trained on more than 40 Cr sales interactions collected over six years.

“Fewer tokens per conversation means less compute per call, which is why our costs have come down even as hardware got more expensive,” Agrawal said.

SquadStack rents dedicated GPUs in India and does not currently plan to buy hardware. Agrawal said owning infrastructure would make more sense at a much larger scale, when utilisation remains high around the clock.

Other companies are looking at similar efficiency measures. Pi-labs’ Zilpelwar said startups are increasingly using smaller, domain-specific models, quantisation and pruning to reduce the amount of memory and computing power needed to run AI workloads.

Similarly, some are ensuring that frontier models are used only when necessary. Routine tasks can be routed to smaller, quantised models, while more complex requests are sent to larger models. This means Indian startups are not focused on deploying the most powerful models, but on extracting the most value from every rupee spent on compute.

[Edited by Shishir Parasher]

item.title: IndiaAI Mission-Backed Chariot AI Unveils 11 Bn Parameter LLM, Speech Models
item.dc:creator: Shraddha Goled
item.description: Chariot AI, a startup developing sovereign foundation model under IndiaAI Mission, has unveiled its Chariot-1 model suite. Launched at a…
item.content:encoded:
Chariot AI, a startup developing sovereign foundation model under IndiaAI Mission, has unveiled its Chariot-1 model suite. Launched at a MeitY event, the AI suite comprises a large language model (LLM) and a text-to-speech (TTS) model.

The Chariot-1 LLM is an 11 Bn parameter mixture-of-experts model, with 4 Bn active parameters per token. It is available in three sizes: 10.7 Bn, 1.7 Bn and 745 Mn parameters, allowing deployment across different computing environments, including data centres, laptops and smartphones. 

Here are the three key AI innovations showcased by Chariot: 

  • IndicShift: Introduces a shared alphabet across 12 Indian scripts, using 350 letters to represent 1,012 characters. It reduces token usage on Indian text by up to 2.5 times compared to OpenAI’s GPT tokeniser and improves model performance on Indian languages by 5–8% on the same compute.
  • Nested Training: Enables three different model sizes to be trained simultaneously in a single training run using one set of weights, allowing deployment across data centres, laptops, smartphones and edge devices. It improves training speed by 62% compared to training the three models separately.
  • Mixture of Vocabularies: Divides the model’s vocabulary into 11 groups, allowing it to score only the relevant group during word selection. This reduces vocabulary entries scored per word by 5.7 times and improves training speed by 38% on the same GPUs, with negligible change in model loss.

The models have been pretrained from scratch in India and incorporate three research innovations aimed at improving computational efficiency, multilingual capabilities and deployment across devices. 

“Designed to advance language understanding and speech generation, the models incorporate novel research innovations aimed at improving computational efficiency, multilingual capabilities and adaptability across different deployment environments,” the government said. 

Alongside these, Chariot AI also launched a text-to-speech (TTS) model that can generate speech in 10 Indian languages. This model is designed to account for context when converting text into speech. It can determine how numbers, dates, currencies, units, URLs and abbreviations should be pronounced, rather than relying on fixed pronunciation rules.

The startup reported over 97% verbalisation accuracy on the Async TTS Pronunciation Benchmark, which comprises 1,029 real-world sentences and 2,251 instances of non-standard text across 42 categories. It also recorded a Hindi character error rate (CER) of 7.60% and an average CER of 6.47% across nine other Indian languages, which Chariot said was the lowest among the systems evaluated in its tests.

Building Chariot AI

Founded earlier this year by Stanford University alumni Parth Sarthi and Suvrat Bhooshan, the Noida-headquartered startup is focusing extensively on foundation models for speech reasoning. 

In an earlier interview with Inc42, Sarthi said that Chariot wants to bring frontier AI research capabilities to India. He identified speech reasoning as a gap in the industry, particularly in a voice-first market such as India.

For context, speech reasoning refers to an AI system’s ability to understand spoken input, interpret context, reason through it and respond or take an appropriate action. The cofounders believe existing models struggle to transfer knowledge across languages and modalities.

“Our goal is to develop novel architectures that address these limitations and demonstrate that frontier AI research can be done in India,” Sarthi said.

Chariot’s longer-term ambition is to build a trillion-parameter model, like AI unicorn Sarvam. The startup is currently working towards a larger model with around 70 Bn parameters to demonstrate that its technology can scale.

Beyond its LLM and TTS model, Chariot is developing tech for automatic speech recognition (ASR) and other speech-related tasks. Sarthi believes speech reasoning could enable applications beyond conventional voice assistants and customer support tools.

“Just as ChatGPT opened up millions of possibilities, a speech reasoning model could allow developers to build applications that we may not have thought of yet,” he said.

While Chariot primarily operates as a B2B provider, its models could also be used by developers to build applications across different use cases. 

“In India, voice AI is taking off. There are several standard use cases, including personal AI assistants and customer support agents that can provide round-the-clock assistance,” Sarthi said. The startup currently has a core team of 12.

Chariot also wants to simplify the technology stack for voice developers by building a single model that can support multiple speech applications. Developers today have to integrate several components, including voice activity detection (VAD), ASR, TTS and language models. Sarthi expects more efficient and affordable models to expand the market for voice AI, invoking the Jevons paradox: as technology becomes cheaper and more efficient, its use tends to increase.

“Applications that were previously not viable because of cost, efficiency or capability constraints will become possible, unlocking new use cases and encouraging more innovation,” he said.

The launch comes amid a push by IndiaAI Mission-backed companies to build homegrown AI models. Earlier today, BharatGen launched vision-language model Patram 1.5 for automating document processing across BFSI, healthcare, government, and other enterprise workflows.

item.title: BharatGen Launches Patram 1.5 To Target Enterprise Document Processing
item.dc:creator: Ankush Das
item.description: BharatGen has launched Patram 1.5, a vision-language model aimed at automating document processing across banking, financial services and insurance (BFSI),…
item.content:encoded:
BharatGen has launched Patram 1.5, a vision-language model aimed at automating document processing across banking, financial services and insurance (BFSI), healthcare, government, and other enterprise workflows.

The model is designed to read and interpret bank statements, KYC forms, medical reports, invoices, and other documents whose layouts and quality can vary widely. BharatGen has also released a playground where users can upload documents and test its capabilities, alongside model weights under an Apache 2.0 licence.

The launch expands BharatGen’s portfolio of AI models spanning text, vision, and speech. The not-for-profit company is anchored at IIT Bombay and backed by the Department of Science and Technology and the IndiaAI Mission,

Reading Beyond The Text

Patram 1.5 treats documents as images, allowing it to interpret text alongside layouts and visual elements rather than relying solely on extracted text.

This is intended to help it process charts, tables, bank statements, and medical reports, where the relationship between different parts of a page can be essential to understanding the information.

One addition, which BharatGen calls “OCR 3.0”, lets users specify both the information they want extracted and the format in which it should be returned. The company also highlighted an abstention capability, designed to flag unclear or missing information rather than generate an unsupported answer.

“The ability to actually say, I don’t know, instead of making up an answer” is critical for business workflows, BharatGen CEO Rishi Bal said during a demonstration.

This capability is particularly relevant to workflows where incorrect information can have financial or regulatory consequences. However, it does not guarantee error-free output.

Bal told Inc42 that Patram 1.5 has been deployed in live data centres across the BFSI and governance sectors, although he did not name the clients. He said the model can run on NVIDIA H100, B200, and L40 GPUs.

Patram Targets The Cost And Privacy Problem

BharatGen’s pitch centres on matching larger models while using fewer resources. Marketed as a 7B model, Patram 1.5 has 7.8 Bn parameters, according to its technical specifications. 

In its own evaluation of 21 vision-language models, Patram 1.5 scored 83 overall, matching Qwen3.5-397B and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash. BharatGen said the latter is 97 times its size.

The company also claims a token-efficiency advantage over Qwen3.5-9B. Across 10 question-answering tests, Patram generated answers using around one twenty-first of the output tokens used by Qwen with its thinking mode enabled, while both scored 85. 

“Not only is Patram smaller than many of the top-performing models, but you’ll also see that it is extremely token efficient as well,” Bal said.

BharatGen is also positioning local deployment as an advantage for organisations handling sensitive documents.

Bal said enterprises can run Patram 1.5 alongside their own data infrastructure instead of sending documents to external AI APIs. Its open weights also allow developers and enterprises to build or fine-tune applications around the model.

The approach forms part of BharatGen’s sovereign AI push, particularly for organisations processing financial, health, and citizen data.

Beyond its own APIs, BharatGen is exploring third-party inference partnerships. Bal said partners have sought secure endpoints hosted inside Indian data centres, which would allow customers to access the model without operating the underlying infrastructure themselves.

“That is something that we’re actively looking at, and it’s something that we will need to provide to make it easier for people to use these models,” he said.

The launch comes amid a broader push by IndiaAI Mission-backed companies to build homegrown AI models, with Chariot AI also unveiling an 11 Bn parameter mixture-of-experts LLM and a text-to-speech model supporting 10 Indian languages.

item.title: India Leads YouTube Take Downs Globally In June Quarter
item.dc:creator: Shrishti Bisht
item.description: Amid growing concern over online content censorship in India, Google-owned social media platform YouTube disclosed that it received the highest…
item.content:encoded:
Amid growing concern over online content censorship in India, Google-owned social media platform YouTube disclosed that it received the highest number of takedown requests in India globally in the April-June 2026 quarter.  

The platform removed 34.41 Lakh videos for violating the platform’s Community Guidelines. The figure represented nearly a third of the 1.11 Cr videos taken down globally during the period, according to YouTube’s latest transparency report.

At the same time, government and court orders seeking content removal from Google platforms have risen sharply. Google received 4,006 such requests from Indian authorities in January-June 2026, covering 65,091 items. This marked a 61.3% increase in requests and a 29.9% rise in the number of items flagged on the platform compared with the preceding six months.

India ranked third globally in the volume of government takedown requests, behind Russia and South Korea. The latest disclosures also detail several contentious cases involving political commentary, news coverage, product reviews and AI-modified content, offering a glimpse into the growing friction between online content regulation and freedom of expression.

Defamation accounted for the largest share of government takedown requests in India, featuring in 2,130, or 53%, of the 4,006 requests received by Google. These covered 33,420 items. Fraud was cited in 332 requests, followed by obscenity or nudity (243), national security (210), electoral law (88) and government criticism (74).

Police made 2,870 requests, or 71.6% of the total, naming 24,334 items. Courts sent another 695 orders, covering 20,407 items.

YouTube received 3,399 requests naming 59,779 content piece, accounting for 91.8% of all items flagged. Google removed 19,883 items for violating local laws and another 1,415 for breaching its own policies. It took no action on 19,402 items.

Some of the cases detailed in Google’s report highlight the contentious nature of these requests.

In one instance, the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting (MIB) ordered YouTube to remove 26 videos from a prominent Indian news channel known for political criticism, citing national security and sovereignty concerns. YouTube initially blocked the entire channel in India.

However, the Delhi High Court later directed the platform to restore access to the channel, observing that restricting an entire channel over a limited number of videos was disproportionate. YouTube restored the channel but took down the 26 videos in question.

AI-generated and modified content emerged as another area of enforcement. Following the notification of the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Amendment Rules, 2026, YouTube received over 400 requests from law enforcement agencies and ministries flagging more than 6,000 videos and channels allegedly containing synthetically generated information (SGI) or AI-modified content featuring high-ranking government officials.

The platform restricted access to the majority of the reported videos and channels in India for violating the amended rules.

India’s Social Media Censorship

The increase in takedown requests comes as India has shortened the time available to intermediaries to comply with government directions.

Under Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules, 2021, platforms must remove or disable access to unlawful information following a valid court order or a reasoned intimation from an authorised government officer.

Amendments, effective February 20, 2026, reduced the compliance window from 36 hours to three hours. Separately, changes effective November 15, 2025, require takedown notices to specify the legal provision invoked, the alleged unlawful act and the exact URL or electronic identifier of the content.

Since then, takedown requests for social media intermediaries have surged significantly. For instance, Meta restricted access to more than 5.44 Mn items across Facebook and Instagram between January and June 2026, compared with around 41,400 in the preceding six months, marking an approximately 131X increase. 

Contesting the digital censorship, Indian Youth Congress (IYC) has been protesting against Meta’s content moderation policies in India. The party has questioned the sharp rise in content restrictions on Meta’s platforms in India and sought greater transparency around its moderation algorithms.

IYC’s national secretary Manu Jain has also moved the Delhi High Court, challenging Rule 4(4) of the IT Rules, 2021, which requires significant social media intermediaries to use automated tools to identify and restrict content identical to material previously blocked under legal orders.

item.title: IndiaMART Settles Legal Dispute With OpenAI
item.dc:creator: Anne Florentyna
item.description: B2B ecommerce company IndiaMART InterMESH has settled its legal dispute with OpenAI pertaining to alleged exclusion of its website and…
item.content:encoded:
B2B ecommerce company IndiaMART InterMESH has settled its legal dispute with OpenAI pertaining to alleged exclusion of its website and seller listings from ChatGPT-generated responses out of court.

The out-of-court settlement of the matter, which was listed in front of the Calcutta High Court, brings the matter to a close after about two years of proceedings.

In an order dated November 17, a division bench comprising Justices Debangsu Basak and Ajay Kumar Gupta recorded the submission made by IndiaMART’s counsel that the parties had reached an out-of-court settlement and that the company was no longer willing to pursue the appeal.

Consequently, the court dismissed the appeal, as ‘not pressed’ and disposed of the connected application.

The court order did not disclose the terms of the settlement or specify whether OpenAI had agreed to restore IndiaMART’s visibility in ChatGPT responses.

Inc42 has reached out to IndiaMART for comments on the development. The story will be updated based on their response.

The dispute dates back to December 2025, when IndiaMART approached the Calcutta High Court alleging that ChatGPT was selectively excluding links to its marketplace while continuing to surface competing B2B marketplaces and individual seller websites.

IndiaMART had argued that OpenAI was relying on the US Trade Representative’s (USTR) Notorious Markets List, which had flagged the company over concerns relating to counterfeiting and piracy. The B2B marketplace contended that the US agency’s findings were not legally binding in India and that OpenAI had relied on the report without giving it an opportunity to present its position.

The company also alleged that the selective exclusion was causing reputational damage, loss of goodwill and commercial injury. It sought a declaration that USTR findings could not be used as grounds to exclude its website and listings from AI-generated search results.

In May, Justice Ravi Krishan Kapur of the Calcutta High Court rejected IndiaMART’s application seeking interim relief against OpenAI.

The court held that IndiaMART had failed to establish a prima facie legal right to demand visibility on ChatGPT and that a private platform could not be compelled to display or promote another company’s links in its responses.

The court also observed that the alleged loss of traffic and potential business was not sufficient to establish an actionable legal injury in the absence of an underlying legal right. The court also acknowledged that the issue required a more detailed examination, including potentially technical and expert evidence.

IndiaMART subsequently challenged the order before the appellate division of the Calcutta High Court. However, the company eventually decided not to pursue the appeal after reaching an out-of-court settlement with OpenAI.

Shares of IndiaMART ended today’s trading session 0.75% higher at ₹1,531.05 apiece on the BSE.

item.title: Urban Company Forays Into AC Market, Opens Pre-Bookings For Native ACs At ₹55,499
item.dc:creator: Gaurav Bagur
item.description: Urban Company has now officially entered India’s residential air conditioner market. In a press release today, the company announced that…
item.content:encoded:
Urban Company has now officially entered India’s residential air conditioner market. In a press release today, the company announced that it has opened pre-bookings for its new products, the Native AC Ultra and Ultra Air lines, exclusively on its app. The products start at ₹55,499 while the full range of products will be announced at launch. 

In terms of cooling performance, Urban Company claims that its ACs are rated to cool a room to 24°C within 21 minutes and maintain full cooling at 47°C. Select models also integrate a HEPA H13 standalone air purifier designed to trap fine dust, pollen, and smoke. 

The products support voice control and come with a remote equipped to sense ambient temperature near the user’s seating position. The hardware is also paired with an app for real-time gas-level and energy tracking. 

Besides, customers buying a Native AC will get a five-year unconditional warranty covering gas refills and a 10-year compressor warranty. 

Urban Company claims that after 1.8 Cr AC service and repair jobs, it identified the most common product failures in the space. These include refrigerant leaks, lack of after-sales service, and efficiency drops when outdoor heat exceeds the 35°C.

“Native AC is designed to solve these problems at the source, and the 5-year unconditional warranty, including gas refills, is how we stand behind it,” said Urban Company’s cofounder and COO Varun Khaitan. 

We had reported on Urban Company’s plans to enter the residential AC market over a year ago. The company’s board officially cleared the expansion earlier this month, approving the expansion of Urban Company’s product brand Native beyond water purifiers and smart locks. 

Separately, Urban Company also raised ₹2,500 Cr this week after launching a qualified institutional placement (QIP) that was oversubscribed by over 6X. 

In terms of capital allocation, ₹600 Cr would be spent on growing its quick home services vertical InstaHelp, ₹540 Cr on marketing, ₹200 Cr on technology development and cloud infrastructure, ₹85 Cr on lease rentals for offices and training centres, and ₹50 Cr on research and development for Native products. 

The fundraise comes on the heels of Urban Company reporting mixed results in Q2 FY27. Consolidated net loss more than tripled to ₹182.5 Cr from ₹59.3 Cr a year earlier as the company ramped up its investments in InstaHelp. On the other hand, operating revenue rose 41.4% YoY to ₹537.3 Cr. 

Shares of Urban Company ended today’s trading session 3.77% higher at ₹170.80 apiece on the BSE.

item.title: Founder Salaries Tracker FY26: How Much Did India’s Startup Founders Earn?
item.dc:creator: Shrishti Bisht
item.description: Thirty-two founders across 22 new-age tech companies earned a combined ₹81.08 Cr in fixed remuneration in FY26, up 3.4% from…
item.content:encoded:
Thirty-two founders across 22 new-age tech companies earned a combined ₹81.08 Cr in fixed remuneration in FY26, up 3.4% from ₹78.43 Cr in FY25. These figures exclude separately disclosed bonuses, incentives, perquisites, and stock-linked compensation. 

Average remuneration per founder rose to ₹2.53 Cr from ₹2.45 Cr. Of the 32 founders tracked, 22 received increases, five saw reductions, and five reported unchanged remuneration.

IndiaMART cofounder Dinesh Agarwal topped the list with ₹5.9 Cr in fixed remuneration, up from ₹5.5 Cr in FY25. Lenskart cofounder Peyush Bansal followed at ₹5.7 Cr, despite a 1.7% decline from ₹5.8 Cr.

Meesho cofounders Vidit Aatrey and Sanjeev Kumar came next at ₹4.8 Cr each, ahead of Ola Electric founder Bhavish Aggarwal at ₹4.5 Cr, IndiaMART cofounder Brijesh Agarwal at ₹4.3 Cr, and Paytm founder Vijay Shekhar Sharma at ₹4 Cr.

At the lower end, EaseMyTrip founder Nishant Pitti drew ₹24 Lakh, followed by Purple Style Labs founder Abhishek Agarwal at ₹72 Lakh, and Nykaa founder Falguni Nayar at ₹74 Lakh.

Who Got A Raise?

Honasa Consumer cofounder Ghazal Alagh recorded the highest percentage increase, with her fixed remuneration rising 60% to ₹2.4 Cr from ₹1.5 Cr.

Zaggle cofounder Avinash Ramesh Godkhindi followed with a 41.9% rise to ₹1.1 Cr from ₹77.5 Lakh. Delhivery cofounder Sahil Barua’s fixed pay increased 21.4% to ₹3.4 Cr from ₹2.8 Cr.

Pitti recorded the steepest percentage decline, with his remuneration falling 75% to ₹24 Lakh from ₹96 Lakh. Aggarwal followed with a 34.8% reduction to ₹4.5 Cr from ₹6.9 Cr.

Nykaa founder Falguni Nayar’s remuneration fell 14% to ₹74 Lakh from ₹86 Lakh, while Swiggy cofounder Sriharsha Majety’s declined 12.5% to ₹1.4 Cr from ₹1.6 Cr.

Beyond The Annual Salary

Annual salaries tell only part of the story. Peyush Bansal received ₹12 Cr in bonuses and performance incentives, more than twice his fixed remuneration, along with perquisites and retirement benefits. Fellow Lenskart cofounder Neha Bansal received ₹6 Cr in bonuses and performance incentives, in addition to ₹2.7 Cr in fixed pay.

MobiKwik cofounders Bipin Preet Singh and Upasana Taku received ₹2.9 Cr each in bonuses and incentives, taking their individual fixed pay and bonuses to ₹6.4 Cr. Honasa Consumer cofounder Varun Alagh received ₹2.4 Cr in performance incentives, equal to his fixed remuneration.

ixigo cofounder Aloke Bajpai received ₹30.2 Lakh in variable pay on top of ₹1.4 Cr in fixed remuneration.

Stock-linked compensation added another dimension. Majety’s disclosed ESOP gains stood at ₹549.3 Cr, while Delhivery cofounder Kapil Bharati recorded ₹6.9 Cr in ESOP gains.

Separately, the disclosed cost of stock options granted to FirstCry founder Supam Maheshwari stood at ₹31.7 Cr. He also received ₹2.1 Cr in perquisites and ₹84 Lakh in performance incentives, alongside ₹1.4 Cr in fixed remuneration. The accrued ESOP expense associated with Bajpai stood at ₹15.7 Cr.

ESOP gains and stock-option costs are different measures and should not be treated as equivalent to cash salaries. The accounting expense associated with stock options does not necessarily represent cash received by a founder during the year.

Inc42 has tracked founders’ remuneration since FY23, covering the startup ecosystem’s shift from the funding boom to the funding winter and, more recently, towards profitability and IPOs.

Building on the FY25 edition, the FY26 tracker examines changes in remuneration, other compensation components, and the financial performance of the companies these founders lead.

Dinesh Agarwal & Brijesh Agarwal | IndiaMART

IndiaMART cofounders Dinesh Agarwal and Brijesh Agarwal together drew ₹10.2 Cr in fixed remuneration in FY26, the highest combined amount among the founder teams tracked.

Dinesh Agarwal’s fixed remuneration rose 7.3% to ₹5.9 Cr from ₹5.5 Cr in FY25, while Brijesh Agarwal’s increased 7.5% to ₹4.3 Cr from ₹4 Cr.

They also received ₹2.4 Cr and ₹1.8 Cr, respectively, in performance incentives.

IndiaMART’s net profit fell 13.8% to ₹474.7 Cr in FY26 from ₹550.7 Cr in FY25. Operating revenue increased 13% to ₹1,569 Cr.

Peyush Bansal | Lenskart 

The Lenskart cofounder and CEO earned ₹5.7 Cr in fixed remuneration in FY26. In addition to his fixed pay, Bansal also received ₹12 Cr in bonus and performance incentives, along with ₹24.04 Lakh in perquisites and ₹7.5 Lakh in retirals.

Lenskart’s net profit rose 69% YoY to ₹500.9 Cr in FY26, while operating revenue increased 33% YoY to ₹8,814 Cr. Its profit growth was aided by operating leverage, premiumisation, and growth in international markets.

Vidit Aatrey & Sanjeev Kumar | Meesho

Meesho cofounders Vidit Aatrey and Sanjeev Kumar each earned ₹4.8 Cr in fixed remuneration in FY26, up 6.7% from ₹4.5 Cr a year earlier.

The data reviewed by Inc42 did not disclose additional perks for either founder.

The ecommerce company’s operating revenue increased 34.5% YoY to ₹12,626 Cr in FY26, while its net loss narrowed 65.6% YoY to ₹1,357.7 Cr.

Its annual transacting user base grew 33% YoY to 26.4 Cr in Q4 FY26, while order volumes increased 43% YoY to 71.7 Cr during the quarter.

Bhavish Aggarwal | Ola Electric 

Ola Electric founder and CMD Bhavish Aggarwal earned ₹4.5 Cr in remuneration in FY26, compared with ₹6.9 Cr in FY25. 

In FY26, the EV maker’s net loss narrowed nearly 20% to ₹1,833 Cr from ₹2,276 Cr in the previous fiscal. Operating revenue nearly halved to ₹2,460 Cr from ₹4,932 Cr.

Bhanu Chopra | RateGain 

RateGain founder and CEO Bhanu Chopra earned ₹3.7 Cr in fixed remuneration in FY26, unchanged from FY25.

The company’s operating revenue rose 69.4% to ₹1,823.6 Cr from ₹1,076.7 Cr, while net profit declined 6.9% to ₹194.4 Cr from ₹208.9 Cr.

Sahil Barua & Kapil Bharati | Delhivery 

Delhivery cofounders Sahil Barua and Kapil Bharati earned ₹3.4 Cr and ₹3.3 Cr, respectively, in fixed remuneration in FY26.

Barua’s fixed pay increased 21.4% from ₹2.8 Cr in FY25, while Bharati’s rose 17.9% from ₹2.8 Cr.

In addition, Barua received ₹33.7 Lakh in performance incentives. Bharati received ₹33 Lakh in performance incentives and ₹6.9 Cr in ESOP gains.

The logistics company’s operating revenue rose 17% YoY to ₹10,486 Cr in FY26, while net profit grew 8% YoY to ₹321 Cr.

Vijay Shekhar Sharma | Paytm 

Paytm founder and CEO Vijay Shekhar Sharma earned ₹4 Cr in fixed remuneration in FY26, unchanged from the previous year. He also received ₹33 Lakh in perquisites.

The fintech company reported its first full-year net profit of ₹552 Cr in FY26, compared with a loss of ₹663 Cr in FY25.

Operating revenue increased 22.3% YoY to ₹8,437 Cr. It also posted an EBITDA of ₹502 Cr, against an EBITDA loss of ₹1,506 Cr in the previous year.

They also received ₹2.9 Cr each in bonuses and incentives, taking their individual fixed pay and bonuses to ₹6.4 Cr.

MobiKwik’s net loss nearly halved to ₹61.9 Cr in FY26 from ₹121.5 Cr in FY25. However, operating revenue declined 4.4% to ₹1,119.2 Cr from ₹1,170.2 Cr.

Gaurav Singh Kushwaha | BlueStone

BlueStone founder and CEO Gaurav Singh Kushwaha received ₹3.4 Cr in remuneration in FY26, up 13.3% from ₹3 Cr in the previous fiscal. The amount includes salary, allowances, perquisites, variable pay, and bonuses.

BlueStone’s operating revenue increased 38% YoY to ₹2,441.2 Cr in FY26. The company reported a net profit of ₹26 Cr, compared with a loss of ₹219.2 Cr in FY25.

Tarun Mehta & Swapnil Jain | Ather

Ather Energy cofounders Tarun Mehta and Swapnil Jain each earned ₹2.1 Cr in fixed remuneration in FY26, up 5% from ₹2 Cr a year earlier. They also received ₹90 Lakh each in variable compensation, taking their individual fixed and variable pay to ₹3 Cr.

item.title: With Nikhil Kamath’s Backing, Can indē wild Stand Out In The BPC Market?
item.dc:creator: Md Zakariya Khan
item.description: Zerodha’s cofounder Nikhil Kamath, via his investment platform WTFund, has backed influencer Diipa Büller-Khosla-led BPC brand indē wild. The undisclosed…
item.content:encoded:
Zerodha’s cofounder Nikhil Kamath, via his investment platform WTFund, has backed influencer Diipa Büller-Khosla-led BPC brand indē wild. The undisclosed funding was finalised in October and announced yesterday (November 25). 

Apart from investing in the brand, Kamath will also be endorsing the brand’s haircare line, Moonlight Growth. This would be the first time Kamath would be endorsing a brand.

“We’re used to seeing celebrities endorse products. But having an investor choose to put his name behind one is a different kind of vote of confidence,” she wrote in an Instagram post today.

The Business Of indē wild

Mumbai-headquartered indē wild was cofounded in 2021 by influencer Khosla and her husband, Oleg Büller-Khosla. 

It is a digital-first beauty and personal care brand that claims to combine traditional Ayurvedic ingredients and rituals with modern skincare and haircare science.

According to the startup’s website, indē wild offers a range of products across haircare, skincare and lip care, among others. Its products are sold through its own online channels and retail partners, including Nykaa, Tira and Sephora.

The startup bids to differentiate its BPC offering by combining traditional Ayurvedic skincare remedies with a high-power influencer marketing engine. 

indē wild’s best-selling product over the years has been Champi Hair Oil, which traces its roots to the early 1980s, when the cofounder’s mother began making hair oil at home in Chennai. 

Inspired by a ritual practised in the Khosla family, she eventually developed the formulation into a family haircare recipe. indē wild was initially launched with a focus on skincare but later decided to double down on the hair oil market.

Over the years, this marketing story has become central to indē wild’s distribution. This also contributed to indē wild’s financial story. As per its latest financial disclosures for the fiscal year FY25, the D2C brand reported a net profit of ₹38.5 Lakh while its revenue more than doubled YoY to ₹25 Ce.

Inc42’s Take: Can indē wild Sustain Itself Amid Intense Competition?

indē wild’s expansion through Sephora and other retail partners gives it an opportunity to reach consumers beyond its digital-first base. However, the bigger challenge for the startup will be converting this initial appeal into sustained demand, repeat purchases and profitable growth, particularly as it expands into international markets.

The landscape, meanwhile, is crowded. indē wild faces competition from established Ayurvedic and premium beauty brands such as Kama Ayurveda, Forest Essentials and Biotique, as well as digital-first players such as Mamaearth, Minimalist, Plum and Pilgrim.

While their positioning and product portfolios differ, they compete for overlapping consumer spending across skincare and haircare. Rising customer acquisition costs, the expense of offline expansion and the need to prove product efficacy could put pressure on indē wild’s margins as it scales.

Its ability to stand out will depend on building a distinct product identity, retaining customers and translating its international visibility into consistent sales, rather than relying mainly on founder-led marketing and its Ayurveda positioning.

item.title: [Update] After Meta Meeting, Congress’ Youth Wing Moves Delhi HC Over Automated Takedown Rules
item.dc:creator: Shrishti Bisht
item.description: Update| November 26, 14:00 IST A day after Congress met Meta executives, Indian Youth Congress (IYC) national secretary Manu Jain…
item.content:encoded:
Update| November 26, 14:00 IST

A day after Congress met Meta executives, Indian Youth Congress (IYC) national secretary Manu Jain approached the Delhi High Court yesterday, challenging a provision under the IT Rules, 2021, that requires social media platforms to use automated tools to identify and block content previously restricted under legal orders.

In his petition, Jain has alleged that Meta is using Rahul Gandhi’s name and photographs as keywords to automatically restrict political content posted by Congress workers on Instagram and Facebook. 

Further, he has submitted notices received by party members between September 29 and November 23, informing them that their posts had been made “unavailable in India”.

The petition cites posts featuring wedding invitations to Gandhi, birthday wishes, tributes to a former prime minister and content related to his University of Chicago lecture. Jain has argued that the posts were ordinary political and personal content, with Gandhi’s name or photograph being their only common element. He has also questioned the absence of specific blocking orders or reasons in the notices.

The plea challenges Rule 4(4) of the IT Rules, which requires significant social media intermediaries to use automated tools to identify and remove content exactly identical to material previously blocked under Rule 3(1)(d). 

Jain has argued that the provision exceeds the powers granted under the Information Technology Act, 2000, and violates the Supreme Court’s safeguards against arbitrary content blocking. 

Original | November 25, 19:39 IST

Amid protests, Meta has reportedly told Congress leaders that it was bound by local laws to take down flagged content and accounts from its platforms. Denying accusations of political favouritism, the tech giant reiterated that it was neutral towards all parties in India.

In a closed-door meeting with Congress leadership today, Meta India executives Aman Jain and Natasha Jog reportedly cited that the removals were in fact linked to its policies on AI-generated content. To this, Congress, whose youth wing (Indian Youth Congress) has been protesting against steep numbers of takedowns on Meta platforms, cited use of AI-generated BJP posts that remained accessible. 

 IYC has called for Meta restore accounts restricted following government directions and explain how its algorithms identify and take down posts. The tech giant, on the other hand, has raised concerns about protests targeting its offices and posters depicting CEO Mark Zuckerberg in RSS traditional attire. 

Meanwhile, IYC workers continued their protest, protesting outside the Bengaluru office today. “Stop dodging accountability, disclose government takedown requests, explain your algorithms and restore unfairly restricted accounts,” IYC said in a post on X. 

With no commitment made by either side, the meeting seems to have ended at a stale mate. The proceedings of the meeting were reported by Reuters. Inc42 has not been able to verify the information independently. We’ll update the story on the basis of comments from the tech giant. 

Meta’s Content Restrictions Surge In India

IYC has been protesting the recent increase in Meta’s content deletion over the past few months. Meta restricted access to more than 5.44 Mn items across Facebook and Instagram between January and June 2026, compared with around 41,400 in the preceding six months, marking an approximately 131X increase, according to its latest transparency disclosures.

The restrictions covered several categories, including online gaming, AI-generated content depicting prominent figures, threats to India’s sovereignty and integrity, gender-based harassment and the promotion of enmity between groups.

Meta has attributed the increase to changes in India’s IT rules, which require platforms to act on government takedown directions within shorter timelines.

India’s social media content moderation framework is primarily governed by the Information Technology Act, 2000, and the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021.

Under Rule 3(1)(d), intermediaries must remove or disable access to unlawful information after receiving a valid court order or a reasoned intimation from an authorised government officer. The provisions cover content relating to national security, public order and India’s sovereignty, among other grounds.

The government has tightened these requirements through successive amendments. In October 2025, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) notified amendments, effective November 15, requiring takedown notices to specify the legal provision invoked, the nature of the alleged unlawful act and the exact URL or electronic identifier of the content. The changes also introduced periodic reviews of government directions by senior officials.

In February 2026, the government further reduced the compliance window for intermediaries. An amendment effective February 20 cut the deadline to remove or disable access to specified unlawful content from 36 hours to three hours after receiving a valid court order or reasoned government intimation.

The shorter deadline has increased pressure on social media platforms to strengthen their content detection and enforcement systems, while raising questions about transparency and the potential for legitimate content to be restricted.

item.title: [Update] MIB Asks Netflix Not To Stream Pakistani Content In India
item.dc:creator: Palak Sharma
item.description: Update | November 26, 13:36 IST The Ministry of Information and Broadcasting (MIB) has reportedly asked Netflix to ensure that…
item.content:encoded:
Update | November 26, 13:36 IST

The Ministry of Information and Broadcasting (MIB) has reportedly asked Netflix to ensure that content originating in Pakistan is not made available to viewers in India, reiterating its advisory dated May 8, 2025.

The development follows complaints and representations received by the Ministry over the possible release in India of Pakistani web series Jo Bachay Hain Sang Samait Lo, starring Fawad Khan and Mahira Khan.

An ANI report, citing sources, further said Netflix had informed the Ministry in June 2025 that it had not made any film or series originating in Pakistan available to its subscribers in India. The Ministry has now asked the streaming platform to stand by that commitment and maintain the position it had communicated earlier.

The latest communication comes amid renewed scrutiny over the availability of Pakistani-origin entertainment content in India, with the Ministry seeking to ensure that Netflix adheres to its existing advisory.

Original| November 25, 15:44 IST

The All Indian Cine Workers Association (AICWA) has written to prime minister Narendra Modi seeking a ban on releasing the Pakistani series “Bachay Hain Sang Samait Lo” on Netflix India on December 4, 2026. 

The body has also demanded a “strong, permanent law” to keep Pakistani content off Indian television, OTT platforms and cinema.

The letter, dated November 24 and signed by AICWA president Suresh Shyamlal Gupta, was shared by news agency ANI on X. It is copied to information and broadcasting minister Ashwini Vaishnaw and to Netflix India.

AICWA’s four demands are listed below: 

  • that the series is not released or streamed in India on December 4 or any other date
  • that all OTT and streaming platforms strictly comply with the May 8, 2025 advisory
  • that the permanent law be enacted
  • that platforms be made to understand that commercial interest can never come before national security and the sentiments of the martyrs’ families

The letter also appeals to Netflix India and other OTT platforms to state clearly in their social media posts that such content will not be shown in India. 

It ends with the line: “No Pakistani face, voice or story has a place on Indian screens.”

Netflix is yet to issue a statement on this. Inc42 has reached out to the company and the story will be updated based on their response.

AICWA claimed that the series stars Pakistani actors — Fawad Khan, Mahira Khan and Hania Aamir — have spoken against India at times of high tension between the two countries. The association said its letter speaks for the “140 Cr people” of the country.

The letter’s central argument is that Netflix’s release would run directly against the government’s stance. AICWA pointed to the information and broadcasting ministry’s May 2025 advisory, which asked OTT platforms and streaming services to stop streaming Pakistan-origin web series, films, songs and podcasts. 

Back then, the ministry said that several terrorist attacks in India have been established to have cross-border linkages with Pakistan-based state and non-state actors. ICWA highlighted that the government itself had banned Pakistani artists from working in the Indian film industry after the recent Pulwama attack. 

Notably, this pattern of cancelling things associated with Pakistan is not only limited to content. Last year, trade body CAIT asked the government to ban Pakistani flags and merchandise on ecommerce platforms. The Central Consumer Protection Authority then issued notices to Amazon, Flipkart, Etsy and three other platforms over the sale of such products.

item.title: Anthropic CEO Accuses Rivals Of Using ‘Human Control’ Slogans Without Tackling AI Risks
item.dc:creator: Shrishti Bisht
item.description: Nasdaq-listed Anthropic’s CEO Dario Amodei has criticised rival AI companies for promoting slogans such as “human control and agency” and…
item.content:encoded:
Nasdaq-listed Anthropic’s CEO Dario Amodei has criticised rival AI companies for promoting slogans such as “human control and agency” and “AI should be just a tool” without adequately addressing the risks of increasingly autonomous systems.

In a lengthy post on X, Amodei accused some rival CEOs of using human agency as a commercial and political pitch without meaningfully differentiating their products or confronting the trade-offs involved.

“What is happening is that there’s a sort of vibes-based commercial and political positioning that some AI CEOs are engaging in,” he wrote.

Amodei’s comments came in response to an Axios report examining differences among AI leaders over whether humans should voluntarily hand some decision-making authority to superintelligent AI systems.

The report said some Anthropic employees believe humans will, and in certain cases should, hand over authority to such systems once they become demonstrably better at making critical decisions. It also cited public pushback from Meta chief AI officer Alexandr Wang and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, who have emphasised retaining human agency.

Amodei rejected suggestions that he supports handing governance to AI, calling it “a terrible idea”. He said AI must remain subject to legitimate democratic processes and that human self-determination should not be sacrificed for efficiency or security.

Governance Versus Task Automation

Amodei argued that the debate conflates two distinct issues – handing governance to AI and using it to automate specific tasks.

While greater automation could drive advances in medicine, transportation, energy, and software, he flagged concerns over job displacement, AI systems autonomously developing more powerful successors, and the reliability of AI-led research into keeping systems aligned with human intentions.

He also cited Anthropic’s stance on autonomous weapons, saying the company had refused to allow its existing models to be used for such weapons despite the threat of legal sanctions.

Amodei argued that rival companies offer broadly similar automation capabilities, questioning whether their public messaging on human control reflects substantive differences in how their products work.

Calls To Slow Development

In September, Amodei published an essay titled ‘We Must Pace The Frontier’, urging AI companies to slow advances in model capabilities so that safety measures and research could keep pace.

The proposal drew public support from Altman, Elon Musk, and Google DeepMind’s Demis Hassabis.

Their backing highlighted broad agreement on the need to manage AI risks, even as their companies continue to compete to build more capable systems.

In a separate development, Altman announced on X yesterday that OpenAI is testing ‘Private Inference’, part of its OpenAI Private Intelligence offering, with a small group of customers.

He said stronger privacy protections would make frontier AI useful for a wider range of work. OpenAI also offers zero data retention (ZDR) with private safety processing, which enables automated safety reviews without giving its personnel access to the underlying content.

OpenAI describes Private Inference as using confidential computing and verifiable controls to protect information during processing.
